newsitem.title: UK: Rescued Briton credits resolve, chocolate for life.
newsitem.headline: Rescued Briton credits resolve, chocolate for life.

text.p: A capsized British yachtsman who defied all odds when he was rescued from icy waters off the Antarctic said on Thursday he owed his life to "sheer determination, a little water and a little chocolate."
Hours after being pulled to safety by the Australian Navy, an ebullient Tony Bullimore told BBC radio: "At the moment, I feel ecstatic."

Bullimore was speaking from the frigate Adelaide, which spotted his yacht's upturned hull drifting in icy waters. Bullimore had cowered inside the boat since capsizing on Sunday during the Vendee Globe round-the-world yacht race, one of the world's most dangerous sporting events.
The former marine, chirpy after his ordeal, gave the Australians "ten out of ten" for saving his life. "It was an incredible rescue. I think it will probably go down in history."
He later told Sky Television: "I think I only just made it. I was deteriorating at quite a reasonable pace."
The Adelaide's captain, Raydon Gates, said the 56-year-old sailor was "acting like a schoolboy" and that it was a miracle he had survived.
Bullimore put his survival down to pluck -- and chocolate.

"It was a horrific, traumatic experience, very difficult," he said. "It was a case of me continuously praying and hoping that there was something happening above the water...It was sheer determination, a little water, a little chocolate: hanging on in there and believing something would happen."
Even British Prime Minister John Major was informed of Bullimore's against-the-odds rescue as he began an Asian tour.
"I think it's an extraordinary story," Major said from India. "Very few people expected a happy outcome but I'm absolutely delighted."
Bullimore's wife Lalel, interviewed at home in southwest England, whooped with delight when told of his rescue.
"We opened a bottle of champagne, we're dancing around the room, shouting and screaming, we hug and we kiss," she said from her home in Bristol, surrounded by some 20 family members.

Lalel said she always knew her husband would be rescued "because he's a survivor." She had no intention of putting a stop to Bullimore's sailing, even as her husband joked he would seek her permission next time he put to sea.
He said: "I cannot wait to be with them (my family) once again -- as long as my wife does not tell me off too much. Next time I will get absolute written permission from my wife."
